title: Who and Where: Describing the Oruro Carnival

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5, and *donde* for places. A relative clause tells you more about a person, thing or place: *los bailarines que llevan máscaras*, *la ciudad donde se celebra el carnaval*. They let you describe a long procession in one flowing sentence. *Que* is the most common; *quien* is only for people.

sections.title: Relative clauses at the carnival
rows: Oruro es la ciudad donde se celebra el carnaval.
Oruro is the city where the carnival is held. (*donde* for a place)
Los bailarines que llevan máscaras representan a los diablos.
The dancers who wear masks represent the devils. (*que* for people)
La morenada es una danza que se baila con trajes muy pesados.
The morenada is a dance that is danced in very heavy costumes. (*que* for a thing)
La Virgen del Socavón, a quien muchos mineros piden protección, tiene un santuario en Oruro.
The Virgin of the Mineshaft, whom many miners ask for protection, has a shrine in Oruro. (*a quien* after a preposition-like *a*)

items.spanish: La diablada es la danza que más se asocia con el carnaval de Oruro.
items.english: The diablada is the dance most associated with the Oruro carnival.

items.spanish: Los músicos que acompañan a los bailarines tocan en las calles.
items.english: The musicians who accompany the dancers play in the streets.

items.spanish: El santuario donde termina el desfile está en el centro de la ciudad.
items.english: The shrine where the parade ends is in the centre of the city.

sections.content: Use *donde* when the clause is about a place, and *quien* (with *a* or another preposition) when it is about a person. Everywhere else *que* works. The relative clause stays next to the noun it describes.
